title: Death (CCC 1005–1014)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mary: the mother whose hand points to her son. Your line was she points to him. Did you point past yourself when someone praised you? Today, we begin the last things: death, judgment, and what comes after. Day three hundred twenty-four.

Ash Wednesday. A line of people shuffles toward the front of the church: office workers on a lunch break, kids in school uniforms, an old man with a cane. One by one, a priest or a minister presses a thumb of gray ash onto each forehead, in the shape of a cross, and says a sentence nobody would put on a greeting card: remember that you are dust, and to dust you shall return. And here's the strange thing. Nobody is required to come, and the line still reaches the back door. Today, why Catholics want to be reminded.
screen: `ASH WEDNESDAY.` → `YOU ARE DUST.` → `PEOPLE LINE UP FOR IT.`

segments.voice: First, the words. On Ash Wednesday the Church uses God's words to Adam, in the Douay-Rheims: "for dust thou art, and into dust thou shalt return." In Latin, memento, homo, quia pulvis es: remember, human, that you are dust. That word memento, remember, gives us today's phrase: memento mori, remember that you will die. Second, what the Church says death is. The Catechism is honest: death is the end of earthly life, and it is natural, and it is also, in Christian teaching, a consequence of sin, something God did not originally want for us. But it says Christ has changed its meaning. Because he died and rose, Catholics say, death is no longer only an end. It can be a passage. Paul could write to the Philippians of "having a desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ." And tradition says that Francis of Assisi, near his own death, added a verse to his Canticle of the Creatures praising God for our Sister Death. Third, why remember it. Not to be morbid. The Catechism says remembering death reminds us that we have limited time to make something of our lives. The old litany of the saints even asks to be spared a sudden and unprepared death: not to be spared death, but to meet it ready. Fourth, what it does to a Tuesday. Think about what changes when you remember you'll die: the grudge looks smaller, the phone call to your mother looks bigger. Old paintings of saints at prayer sometimes put a skull on the desk, beside the book and the candle. Not fear. Focus.
screen: `DUST THOU ART.` · `A PASSAGE, NOT ONLY AN END.` · `SISTER DEATH.` · `LIMITED TIME: LIVE IT.` · then, large: `MEMENTO MORI.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: what you'd want said of you. Settle, and breathe. Imagine, gently, the day people gather to remember you. Not the sad part. Just the words. What would you want someone who loved you to say? Not your job title. Something like: she always had time. He made people laugh. They never gave up on anyone. Let one sentence come. Hold it. Later today, write it down. If you pray, you can ask for help to become it. The bell holds the time.
Memento mori. Latin for remember that you will die: an old Christian practice of keeping death in view, not out of fear, but to live well. Today's word.
Your line: remember you will die. Today, write down your one sentence, and do one thing that makes it a little more true. Day three hundred twenty-four.

howItsDone: Catholics receive ashes on Ash Wednesday with the words remember that you are dust, pray for a holy death, and many keep November as a month of remembering the dead.

notes: Douay-Rheims Genesis 3:19 and Philippians 1:23 given from memory; confirm wording.

The Ash Wednesday formula is given in English and Latin as the rite's words ('memento, homo, quia pulvis es'); the English is described, not cited to a translation. The Missal also allows 'repent, and believe in the Gospel'.
'Some years it's one of the busiest days' for Ash Wednesday attendance: a common observation; soften if needed.
Saints keeping skulls on their desks: a common motif in art (e.g. Jerome, Francis); stated generally.
CCC 1005–1014 paraphrased; confirm. 'Remember to die' as a literal gloss of memento mori.
